slides.headline: This monarch lives months, not weeks.
slides.sub: Meet the generation built for the flight south

slides.headline: Summer monarchs live fast
slides.body: Breeding adults live about 2–5 weeks: they mate, lay eggs and die. Up to four generations follow each other every summer, each moving further north.

slides.label: months: the lifespan of the overwintering generation
slides.body: The last generation of the year migrates south. These adults put breeding on hold (reproductive diapause) and can live six to nine months.

slides.label: and more: the eastern monarchs' fall flight to Mexico
slides.body: They winter in oyamel fir forests in central Mexico's mountains, 2,400–3,600 m above sea level. Pictured: a wild roost at Piedra Herrada, Mexico.

slides.headline: Steering by the sun
slides.body: Migrants navigate with a time-compensated sun compass. The clock that corrects for the sun's movement across the sky sits in their antennae.

slides.headline: Vulnerable, and still declining
slides.body: The IUCN listed the migratory monarch as Endangered in 2022, then reassessed it as Vulnerable in 2023. Its population trend is still decreasing.

caption:
Most monarch butterflies (Danaus plexippus) live a few weeks, but the last generation of summer can live six to nine months.

That long-lived generation makes the migration. Monarchs west of the Rocky Mountains fly a shorter route, about 500 to 1,600 km, to hundreds of groves along the California coast, where they cluster in eucalyptus, Monterey pine and Monterey cypress trees. In spring the journey north is a relay, taking 3 to 4 generations to reach the northern US and Canada.

Swipe for how one generation does it all. Sources on the last slide.

Source: USDA Forest Service; US Fish & Wildlife Service; Merlin et al. (2009), Science; IUCN Red List (2023).
